en: The Mahāvaipulya Sūtra on Entering the Inconceivable Wisdom and Virtue of the Tathāgata, one fascicle;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Śikṣānanda of Khotan during the Great Tang Dynasty.
Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was staying in the Hall of Universal Radiance at the Site of Enlightenment in the kingdom of Magadha—a place arisen from the accumulation of immeasurable merit, such that all who saw it could not fail to give rise to great joy and delight, forever free from any thought of contempt or disparagement.

The Buddha sat upon a lion throne of precious lotuses therein, realizing pure and perfect enlightenment. His conduct was non-dual; he dwelt where all Buddhas dwell, attaining equality with all Buddhas and reaching the state of unobstructed, non-retrogressive Dharma.
In all their activities, they cannot be overcome; they constantly perform the work of Buddhas without ever resting.
Realizing that phenomena are signless, they abide in the inconceivable; regarding all that arises throughout the three periods of time, they understand them to be without distinction.

His body pervades all worlds; his wisdom penetrates all phenomena, never experiencing confusion; he awakens to all conditioned activities and severs the net of all doubts; his body is subtle and wondrous, beyond all conceptual differentiation.

Having reached the ultimate shore of non-dual wisdom, they are venerated by all Bodhisattvas; abiding in the undifferentiated liberation of the Tathāgatas, they enter the Buddha’s stage of equality, which is without center or periphery; penetrating the entire dharma-realm of space, they constantly turn the wheel of Dharma throughout kalpas as endless as the future.

He was accompanied by an assembly of sixty-two billion great bhikṣus, all of whom had thoroughly realized the true nature of all phenomena (*dharmasatyalakṣaṇa*), which is equal in its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) like empty space, free from any dependence or attachment, and forever liberated from the shrouds and entanglements of all afflictions (*kleśa*).

They are able to enter into the wisdom and skillful means of all Tathāgatas; within a single dharma, they comprehend all dharmas; non-conceptual wisdom is ever present before them; they constantly and diligently cultivate the path toward the knowledge of all modes; their minds never regress; they have all achieved the wisdom that reaches the other shore; and regarding all objects and the skillful means they employ, there is nothing that is not fully perfected.

Their names were Śāriputra, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Mahākātyāyana, Mahākāśyapa, Nadīkāśyapa, Gayākāśyapa, Mahākausthila, Revata, Aniruddha, Subhūti, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra, Gavāmpati, Cūḍapanthaka, Vatsasagotra, Khadiravaniya, Śreṣṭhidatta, Mahākauṣṭhila, Nanda, Rāhula, and Ānanda; these and other great disciples served as the leaders.

Furthermore, he was accompanied by sixty billion bhikṣuṇīs—all of whom had long since accumulated pure, white dharmas, drawn near to the Buddha’s knowledge of all modes, and mastered skillful means; who had realized that all dharmas are without self-nature and without marks, and dwelt securely in the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi); who understood that all dharmas are neither born nor extinguished and require no elimination or abandonment; and who abided in the inconceivable samādhi of liberation, manifesting various deportments and physical forms according to the needs of sentient beings to be tamed, yet remaining free from any discrimination therein.
They were headed by Mahāprajāpatī and Yaśodharā.

Furthermore, he was accompanied by bodhisattva-mahāsattvas as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably many hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of ten buddha-fields. All of them were in their final birth before Buddhahood (*ekajātipratibaddha*), having gathered here from other world-systems. They were all able to universally enter the worlds of the ten directions and had attained the skillful means and wisdom of the path to *nirvāṇa*. They dwelt securely in the bodhisattva dharma-gate of observation and accomplishment for the sake of all sentient beings, gathering in all beings and causing them to sever all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) and grasping. They thoroughly understood that all phenomena are neither infinite nor finite, and they knew that the karmic fruits of good and evil for all sentient beings are ultimately ungraspable, yet are never lost or destroyed.

Furthermore, they are able to thoroughly investigate the mental dispositions, afflictions, faculties, and spheres of activity [of beings]; they fully uphold the words and meanings of all dharmas taught by the Tathāgatas of the three periods of time without any forgetfulness; they penetrate all conditioned and unconditioned phenomena, as well as mundane and supramundane dharmas; and they achieve the wheel of wisdom of the Buddhas of the three periods of time.

In every moment of thought, they manifest the signs of passing away from celestial palaces, taking birth, leaving home, practicing austerities, proceeding to the Bodhi tree, subduing Māra and attaining Buddhahood, turning the wheel of the True Dharma, and entering parinirvāṇa; yet they never weary of or abandon any sentient being, awakening them and causing them to resolve upon the Great Bodhicitta. They are able to enter the objects perceived by the minds of all sentient beings through the objects perceived by the mind of a single sentient being; having accomplished spontaneous wisdom (*svayambhū-jñāna*), they assume the body of a bodhisattva, never regressing from the conduct of omniscience (*sarvajña-caryā*). Although they constantly practice, they remain without any [deliberate] activity.

They are able to remain in the world for immeasurable eons to preach the Dharma for the sake of a single sentient being, protecting and upholding the treasury of the Dharma and continuing the lineage of all Buddhas.

In places where no Buddha dwells, they manifest the appearance of a Buddha in the world as many times as there are sentient beings; they demonstrate the attainment of perfect enlightenment, sit cross-legged, pervade the ten directions, and bring great wisdom to full completion.
They thoroughly purify all defiled lands and eliminate all karmic obstacles of bodhisattvas;
within the dharma-realm of empty space, they are fully endowed with all merits.
Realizing the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) without any obstruction, one attains the seal of the wisdom of equality regarding all phenomena.
By this seal, one knows that the self-nature of all phenomena is equal; thus, whatever is seen or heard is like a shadow or an echo.

Abiding in the Samādhi of the Sovereign Play of the Inconceivable Liberation, they have accomplished the dhāraṇī-gate that gives rise to the marks and signs of all Buddhas; they possess the pure vows and conduct of the Buddhas of the three periods of time, and have achieved the sublime aspirations of Samantabhadra.
When the Buddhas appear in the world, they all go to that place and respectfully entreat him.
Within a single hair-path, he manifests all worlds; within a single hair-path, he manifests the ten directions, from his initial descent into birth until his final entry into parinirvāṇa.
They manifest the assemblies of all Buddhas of the ten directions within a single assembly of a Buddha;
and from a single assembly of a Buddha, they manifest the assemblies of all Buddhas of the ten directions.

He manifests the realms of the ten directions within his own body, and within his own body he manifests the bodies of all sentient beings, expounding immeasurable essential teachings for them accordingly.
He manifests the bodies of all Buddhas entering the body of a single Buddha, and the body of a single Buddha entering the bodies of all Buddhas;
within the body of a single sentient being he manifests the bodies of immeasurable sentient beings, and within the bodies of all sentient beings he manifests the body of a single sentient being.
Within the body of one lifetime, they manifest the bodies of three lifetimes; within the bodies of three lifetimes, they manifest the body of one lifetime.
They manifest the past life entering the future life, and by means of the future life enter the past life;
they enter the present life by means of the past life, and enter the past life by means of the present life.
Entering deep meditative absorption within a single body, they arise in immeasurable and innumerable bodies;
entering deep meditative absorption in immeasurable and innumerable bodies, they arise in a single body.
Within the body of a single Buddha, he manifests the bodies of all sentient beings; within the bodies of all sentient beings, he manifests the body of a single Buddha.
Within the bodies of sentient beings, he manifests the pure Dharma-body; within the pure Dharma-body, he manifests the bodies of sentient beings.
They manifest a single Buddha-field and its adornments within all pure fields;
they manifest all Buddha-fields and their adornments within a single pure field;

they cause the worlds of the ten directions to enter a single pore, manifesting for all sentient beings the power of the vows of all Buddhas, and universally appearing the unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment throughout the ten directions according to those who may be transformed and delivered.
Throughout incalculable eons, they practice the bodhisattva path in each and every world without rest;
within a single atom, they contain boundless, immeasurable, and incalculable worlds, ensuring that all sentient beings therein experience no crowding or constraint.
He condenses immeasurable and inconceivable eons into a single moment, and expands a single moment into immeasurable and inconceivable eons.

Within a single kṣaṇa, throughout all worlds in the ten directions, he manifests various modes of conduct and deportment according to those beings who are ready to be tamed—whether born from eggs, from wombs, from moisture, or by transformation; whether with form or without form, with color or without color; whether legless, two-legged, four-legged, or many-legged; including devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, Śakra, Brahmā, the World Protectors, humans, non-humans, and so forth—yet his body and mind remain free from the activity of discrimination.
All these bodhisattvas have attained such skillful means as well as other immeasurable, asaṃkhyeya merits.

Their names are: Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, Samantanetra Bodhisattva, Samantavikurvita Bodhisattva, Samantamati Bodhisattva, Samantacakṣus Bodhisattva, Samantaprabha Bodhisattva, Samantajñāna Bodhisattva, and Samantāvabhāsa Bodhisattva.
The Bodhisattva Universal Banner, the Bodhisattva Universal Awakening, the Bodhisattva Great Swift, the Bodhisattva Great Swift-Holder,
the Bodhisattva Great Supernatural Transformation, the Bodhisattva King of Great Supernatural Transformations, the Bodhisattva Great Diligence,
the Bodhisattva Great Valor, the Bodhisattva Great Exertion, and the Bodhisattva Great Exertion.
Bodhisattva Bala, Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, Bodhisattva Mahāgandhahastin,
Bodhisattva Mahācandra, Bodhisattva Sucandra, Bodhisattva Guṇacandra, Bodhisattva Ratnacandra,
Bodhisattva Samantacandra, Bodhisattva Dharmavimalacandra, Bodhisattva Vairocanacandra, and Bodhisattva Yaśaścandra.
Bodhisattvas: Radiant Moon Bodhisattva, Full Moon Bodhisattva, Brahma-Sound Bodhisattva,
Brahma-Lord Thunder-Sound Bodhisattva, Earth-Sound Bodhisattva, Dharma-Domain Sound Bodhisattva,
Destroyer-of-All-Māras-Sound Bodhisattva, Resounding-Dharma-Drum-Sound Bodhisattva, Universal-Awakening-Sound Bodhisattva, and Non-Differentiation [Bodhisattva].
Bieyin Bodhisattva, Dishangyin Bodhisattva, Bi-yiqieshengyin Bodhisattva, Pingdengzang Bodhisattva,
Liouzuzang Bodhisattva, Gongdezang Bodhisattva, Guangmingzang Bodhisattva, Baozang Bodhisattva,
Yuezang Bodhisattva, Rizang Bodhisattva, and Risheng Bodhisattva.
Gaganagañja Bodhisattva, Padmagarbha Bodhisattva, Prajñāgarbha Bodhisattva, Mahāprajñā Bodhisattva, Jñānavijaya Bodhisattva,
Yaśaḥprajñā Bodhisattva, Anuttaraprajñā Bodhisattva, Vardhamānaprajñā Bodhisattva,
Amitaprajñā Bodhisattva, Vipulaprajñā Bodhisattva, Buddhaprajñā Bodhisattva, and... [no further names provided].
The Bodhisattva Kṣayajñāna, the Bodhisattva Sāgarabuddhi, the Bodhisattva Merupradīpa, the Bodhisattva Mahāpradīpa,
the Bodhisattva Dharmapradīpa, the Bodhisattva Daśadigavabhāsapradīpa, the Bodhisattva Samantapradīpa, the Bodhisattva Sarvatamovighātapradīpa,
the Bodhisattva Sarvatrajyotipradīpa, and the Bodhisattva Niścayāvabhāsapradīpa.
...Candrapradīpa Bodhisattva, Sūryapradīpa Bodhisattva, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva, Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva,
Mahāsthāmaprāpta Bodhisattva, Vajragarbha Bodhisattva, Guṇagarbha Bodhisattva, Apāyāntaja Bodhisattva,
Bhaiṣajyarāja Bodhisattva, Bhaiṣajyasamudgata Bodhisattva, and Meghasvara [Bodhisattva].
The Bodhisattva, the Bodhisattva Flower-Crested, the Bodhisattva Sunlight, the Bodhisattva Stainless Valor,
the Bodhisattva Vajra-Wisdom, the Bodhisattva Extinction of All Obscurations, the Bodhisattva Subduer of Māras, the Bodhisattva Jewel-Tuft, the Bodhisattva Thousand Lights,
the Bodhisattva Subduer of Great Māras, the Bodhisattva Difficult to Behold, and the Bodhisattva Difficult...
The Bodhisattva Prostrate, the Bodhisattva Immeasurable, the Bodhisattva Supreme Wisdom, the Bodhisattva Extinction of Evil Destinies,
the Bodhisattva Maitreya, and other such Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas were the leaders.

Furthermore, there were immeasurable, inconceivable, and incalculable numbers of devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, Śakras, Brahmās, and World-Protectors, all of whom had come together from the buddha-fields of the ten directions.

At that time, there were also ten billion gods of the six heavens of desire, headed by Māra, his sons, and merchant lords, who together with immeasurable retinues of celestial beings, went to where the Buddha was, in order to see, prostrate to, make offerings to, and listen to the Dharma from the Tathāgata.

Furthermore, there were ten billion Great Brahmā Kings, up to and including ten billion Akaniṣṭha Devas, with Mahesvara as their leader; they too, together with immeasurable retinues of devas, went to the place where the Buddha was, in order to see, prostrate to, make offerings to, and listen to the Dharma from the Tathāgata.

Furthermore, there were ten billion assemblies of the eight classes of supernatural beings, as well as immeasurable numbers of humans, non-humans, upāsakas, and upāsikās, each accompanied by their retinues, who went together to the place where the Buddha was, in order to see the Tathāgata, pay homage, make offerings, and listen to and receive the Dharma.

Furthermore, all the deities of grasses, trees, forests, and various medicinal herbs; the deities of Mount Meru, Mahāmeru, Mucilinda, Mahāmucilinda, the Snowy Mountains, the Iron Ring Mountains (*Cakravāḍa*), and all other mountains;

as well as all the deities of rivers, oceans, ponds, lakes, kingdoms, cities, and villages, together with the deities of the palaces of the eight classes of beings—all approached the place where the Buddha was, accompanied by their retinues, in order to see the Tathāgata, pay him homage, make offerings, and listen to the Dharma.

Furthermore, there were ten billion suns, moons, and devas, as well as the Nāga King Anavatapta, each surrounded by immeasurable retinues, who together proceeded to the place where the Buddha was, in order to see, prostrate to, make offerings to, and listen to the Dharma from the Tathāgata.
By the Buddha’s spiritual power, this great assembly was free from mutual obstruction and experienced no crowding.

At that time, the World-Honored One’s radiance shone forth brilliantly, eclipsing the entire gathering; it was like the full moon on the fifteenth day, when the clouds and mists have been cleared away, its brilliant light outshining all the stars, and like Mount Sumeru, the king of mountains, abiding firmly and immovably.
The Tathāgata’s radiance universally eclipses all the Śakras and Brahmās among the devas; his loftiness, excellence, and preeminence are likewise so.
At that time, the youth Mañjuśrī addressed the Bodhisattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin, saying:
"Do you know that the Tathāgata is now dwelling here, his body unmoving?"
He replied: "Mañjuśrī!
Although the Tathāgata now remains unmoving within this assembly, there are devas and humans who see him leaving the household life and practicing asceticism."

Or they see him proceeding to the foot of the Bodhi tree and taking his place at the site of enlightenment, where he subdues the hosts of Māra and attains equal and perfect awakening; then all the devas, nāga kings, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, Śakra, Brahmā, and the world-protectors together praise him, saying:
"Excellent!
"The Great Master is able to overcome all enemies!
Or they see Śakra, Brahmā, and the world-protecting devas entreating him to preach the Dharma;
or they see him preaching the Dharma of generosity for their sake.
In some cases, they see [the Buddha] teaching the dharmas of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, wisdom, skillful means, powers, vows, and knowledge;
in some cases, they see him teaching the vehicle of the śrāvakas;
and in some cases, they see him teaching the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas.
In some instances, he sees [the Buddha] preaching the Dharma of the Unsurpassed Vehicle;

in others, he sees [the Buddha] preaching the Dharma concerning rebirth among animals, hungry ghosts, the realm of Yama, the Heaven of the Four Great Kings, the Heaven of the Thirty-three, and even up to the Brahma palaces;
or he sees [the Buddha] preaching the Dharma for rebirth in the human realm.
Or they see [the Tathāgata] preaching the Dharma for becoming a Wheel-Turning King.
"Furthermore, Mañjuśrī!
Within this assembly, some see the body of the Tathāgata to be one fathom in height."
Or one *krośa*, or two *krośas*;

or half a *yojana*, or one *yojana*, or two *yojanas*, or ten *yojanas*, or a hundred, a thousand, or ten thousand *yojanas*; or they may see fifty thousand, a hundred thousand, a million, or five million, even up to seeing more than all conceivable numbers of *yojanas*.

“Some see the Buddha’s body as the color of true gold; some as the color of lapis lazuli; some as the color of indranīla mani; some as the color of mahānīla mani; some as the color of light-radiant mani; some as the color of red-lotus mani; some as the color of śakrābhilagna mani; some as the color of vajra-light mani; some as the color of celestial-light mani; some as the color of sun-moon-light mani; some as the color of crystal mani; some as the color of sphatika mani; some as the color of vaśavarti-rāja mani; some as the color of saṃkusumita-raśmi mani; some as the color of siṃhakaṇṭha mani; some as the color of siṃhadhvaja mani; some as the color of sāgaravihāra-viśuddhaprabhā mani; or some as the color of cintāmaṇi.”
According to the various sentient beings who should see the Tathāgata in such-and-such physical forms to be tamed, what they see differs from one another;
according to those who are matured by hearing the Tathāgata preach this or that Dharma, what they hear differs from one another;
and according to those who practice based on whichever teaching, each acts as instructed and all attain accomplishment.

“Mañjuśrī! Suppose that throughout the ten directions, in immeasurable, inconceivable, and incalculable worlds, they were filled with devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, Śakras, Brahmās, world-protectors, humans, and non-humans, just like a grove of bamboo, or stalks of sugarcane, or sesame seeds.”

If there are sentient beings who should be tamed by seeing the Tathāgata, they see the Buddha’s physical form appearing differently for each, facing them directly at a distance of one fathom; he preaches the Dharma for them, and through practicing according to what was taught, they all attain accomplishment.
Although the Tathāgata performs such manifold deeds, he manifests them spontaneously and without discrimination. "Mañjuśrī!
It is like the full moon at midnight; all sentient beings within Jambudvīpa each see the lunar disc appearing before them, yet that moon has never formed any thought or discrimination."
"May all sentient beings each behold my manifestation.
It is the natural law that such an event occurs.
The Tathāgata is likewise; although he manifests universally before all sentient beings, he does not engage in discrimination.
"May all sentient beings see me dwelling before them.
Yet, according to those among sentient beings who are ready to be tamed, each sees the Buddha appearing right before them.
Why is this? Because it accords with the unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*) of sentient beings as they correspond to their capacities. "Mañjuśrī!..."

Just as all sentient beings, by the power of the fruits of superior, middling, and inferior karma, perform various conditioned activities that likewise fall into these three grades, yet these activities themselves never give rise to the threefold discrimination;
rather, it is solely due to karma that there naturally arise such superior, middling, and inferior grades of conditioned activities.

The Tathāgata is likewise: by the power of the karmic fruits of sentient beings, each perceives the Buddha according to their own [capacity]; yet the Tathāgata possesses no thoughts of superior, middling, or inferior, for such manifestations occur spontaneously and in accordance with reality.
“Mañjuśrī! It is like placing a pure crystal upon various garments so that it takes on their diverse colors:
if placed upon a yellow garment, it appears as yellow;”
When placed upon blue or red cloth, it appears as blue or red; yet, although it assumes those colors according to where it is set, this pure crystal remains ultimately without discrimination.
The Tathāgata is likewise: through the karmic responses of sentient beings, he manifests various colors.
If there are sentient beings who should see a golden color to be tamed, they shall see a golden color.

If there are those who are to be tamed by the colors of various jewels—such as lapis lazuli, pearl, sapphire, great blue gem, the *saṃghātaprabhāsa* maṇi, the *sāgaravāsaviśuddhaprabha* maṇi, the *siṃhamālā* maṇi, the *siṃhadhvaja* maṇi, the *vidyutpradīpa* maṇi, or the *sphāṭika* maṇi—the Tathāgata appears to them with the appearance of such various jewel-colored forms.
Or, if there are those who are to be tamed by Śakra, Brahmā, or the World-Protectors (*lokapāla*), they see the Tathāgata appearing in the form of Śakra, Brahmā, or the World-Protectors.

In this way, even unto those who should be tamed by the appearances of hells, hungry ghosts, animals, the realm of Yama, or the realms of form and formlessness; or by the modes of birth—whether from eggs, from a womb, from moisture, or by transformation; or by the physical forms of those with form, those without form, those with perception, those without perception, or those with neither perception nor non-perception—whichever mode of existence, deportment, or physical appearance may serve to tame them, the Tathāgata appears in such various forms and appearances.
Yet the Buddha has never made a discriminatory thought, saying:
"Let these sentient beings see only gold and not lapis lazuli;
let them see only lapis lazuli and not sapphire."
"In this way, up until one sees only the lion-garland maṇi, one does not see the color of the lion-banner maṇi.
Although there is no such conceptual discrimination of differing thoughts, these various forms and appearances naturally manifest in all places accordingly.
“Mañjuśrī! For example, in the place where the sovereign maṇi-king is produced, no iron is born; yet that sovereign maṇi-king never thinks:
‘Let only I be produced in this jewel-place, and let no iron be produced.’”
"However, in that place of jewels, iron does not arise of its own accord.

It is the same with the Buddha-land where the Tathāgata is born: it naturally lacks all heterodox doctrines and contentious arguments, all evil bandits and disturbances, the five crimes of immediate retribution, the ten unwholesome karmas, and the teachings of non-Dharma kings. Furthermore, it lacks all light from the sun, moon, various devas, maṇi jewels, fire, lightning, and so forth, as well as the divisions of time such as moments, days, months, and years—except for the manifestations of the Buddha’s transformations to convert sentient beings; though these appear, they are devoid of conceptual discrimination."
"Because of sentient beings, these various phenomena naturally arise. Mañjuśrī!
It is like the light of a great sapphire gem: all who are touched by it take on the color of that great blue gem, yet the gem itself never has any thought of differentiation."
The Tathāgata is likewise: those who encounter the light of the Buddha’s mental engagement as an object of focus all become the embodiment of omniscience.
Yet the Buddha has no conceptual discrimination or dualistic thought; such phenomena arise spontaneously and naturally.

“Mañjuśrī! Just as when a great beryl gem is well-polished and refined, whatever various ornaments for the hands, feet, head, or neck are placed near it, they all become clearly visible through the power of that gem;
so too is the Tathāgata: wherever there are practitioners who abide in his conduct and deportment, by the Buddha’s power, their own practice is made to increase and excel.”
Yet the Buddha never stirs a thought or engages in discrimination; such things arise spontaneously.
"Mañjuśrī! It is like all manner of grasses, shrubs, and trees that depend upon the earth to dwell and each attain growth, yet the earth itself has no various discriminations whatsoever."

The Tathāgata is likewise: he causes all the roots of goodness of sentient beings to abide in the Tathāgata and each to increase, yet in reality, he never has any conceptual discrimination; such things arise spontaneously.

“Mañjuśrī! It is like a great cloud that universally covers all grasses, trees, and forests, raining down sweet rain equally. Wherever this water of a single flavor reaches, it causes all the grasses and trees to grow; yet their various colors and flavors differ from one another. That cloud never makes any distinction, yet such various differences arise naturally.”

The Tathāgata is likewise: he raises the cloud of perfect enlightenment to universally cover all, and according to the various roots of goodness previously accumulated by sentient beings, their various aspirations and delights, their various faiths and understandings, and their various liberations, he equally pours down the rain of Dharma. He causes all the roots of goodness of sentient beings to grow, each according to its own power. Yet the Tathāgata does not engage in discriminative thought, saying:
"I shall cause the roots of goodness of these sentient beings to give rise to the wisdom of Śrāvakas;
I shall cause the roots of goodness of these sentient beings to give rise to the wisdom of Pratyekabuddhas."
I shall cause the roots of goodness of these sentient beings to give rise to the wisdom of the Tathāgata;
I shall cause the roots of goodness of these sentient beings to give rise to birth in the heavens of the Four Great Kings and the Heaven of the Thirty-three, and so on up to the Śuddhāvāsa heavens;
I shall cause the roots of goodness of these sentient beings to attain the status of kings, as well as various other states of birth among human beings.

"However, although the Buddha is free from various conceptual discriminations, in accordance with the roots of goodness, aspirations, and the power of devotion accumulated by sentient beings, these various phenomena naturally arise; this is because the Buddha has already abandoned all attachments to objects and is devoid of discrimination."

“Mañjuśrī! Just as when the sun first appears, it emits immeasurable billions of hundreds of thousands of rays of light, destroying all darkness throughout Jambudvīpa; although the sun does not discriminate or say, ‘I shall destroy the darkness,’ the act of destroying the darkness occurs spontaneously.”

The sun-disk of the Tathāgata is likewise: having appeared in the world, it emits immeasurable billions of rays of wisdom-light to eliminate the darkness of all worldly views. Except for those instances where the Buddha’s majestic power manifests to bring sentient beings to maturity, the Tathāgata does not engage in discriminative thought, saying:
"I shall cause sentient beings to see; I have manifested what is to be destroyed, and I shall destroy what remains."
"In all places, these various things arise spontaneously because the Buddha has already abandoned all attachment to places and is free from conceptual discrimination. Mañjuśrī!..."
It is like a magician who conjures various forms; although these take on diverse shapes and types, the illusion itself is without discrimination and cannot be described.
It has no arising and no ceasing, no letters and no sounds, no location and no substance, and no marks—it is inconceivable.
It is non-dual and without activity, without equal and without counterpart, existing only as these various manifestations produced by the magician.
The Tathāgata is likewise: for the sake of sentient beings, he enters into various modes of conduct and spheres of activity, such that all may see him.

Yet in reality, the Tathāgata is ineffable, without arising or ceasing, without letters or sounds, without location, without nature or characteristics, non-dual, and without activity; he is equal to the true Dharma-realm and cannot be grasped or encountered.

“Mañjuśrī! For example, because the sun reflects upon Mount Sumeru, the sentient beings of the four continents may see it first rising, or see it at midday, or see it gradually setting, or see it first disappearing, or see it at midnight, or see it gradually breaking dawn;
yet there is but one solar disk, which appears differently to the various sentient beings according to their location within the four worlds.”
The sun is without discrimination; it is merely due to the obstruction of mountains that what is seen in the four continents naturally differs from one another.
It is the same with the Tathāgata: within a single assembly, some may see the Tathāgata about to attain perfect enlightenment or having already attained perfect enlightenment;
some may see him about to enter nirvāṇa or having already entered nirvāṇa.
Some see him having already attained Buddhahood for ten years, or even for unspeakable eons;
some see him having already entered Nirvana for ten years, or even for hundreds of thousands of billions of eons;
or they see the Tathāgata remaining in the world preaching the Dharma for ten or twenty years, or forty years.
Some see the persistence of phenomena, while others see the cessation of phenomena.
Yet the Buddha never entertains any conceptual discrimination; it is solely due to sentient beings that these various occurrences arise spontaneously.

“Mañjuśrī! It is like a great wind blowing over Jambudvīpa, causing all the grasses, trees, branches, and leaves to become disordered, falling or rising toward the east, west, south, or north. Yet these grasses and trees ultimately have no various discriminations of their own; it is solely due to the wind that various forms arise.”

The Tathāgata is likewise; though eternally free from conceptual discrimination, by the power of sentient beings, within every moment of thought he perceives the arising of such immeasurable marks of various practices and dignified deportment, even extending to his mental engagement with all sentient beings, whereby for as many eons as there are, they attain the severance of rebirth in the realms of hell, animals, hungry ghosts, and Yama.
“Mañjuśrī! The Tathāgata has accomplished such immeasurable and subtle merits.
“Mañjuśrī! [he continued.]

Regarding the object of a single moment of mental attention of the Tathāgata, even great bodhisattvas who have dwelt for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of nayutas of kalpas in the inconceivable samādhi of liberation cannot know its limit of merit.

“Mañjuśrī! It is like the orb of the sun rising from the great ocean and dwelling in the midst of space, emitting immeasurable billions of nayutas of rays that universally illuminate all cities and villages, shattering the great darkness, drying up muddy pools, causing all grasses, trees, thickets, and forests to grow and fully ripen, initiating all manner of activities, and casting its light and shadows throughout all rivers and ponds, yet never departing from its original state.
Although on this day there are no various conceptual discriminations, such phenomena naturally manifest.

The Tathāgata is likewise: having emerged from the ocean of all existence and dwelling in the space of the Dharma, he emits immeasurable billions of rays of wisdom-light that universally illumine all worlds throughout the ten directions, extinguishing the cataracts of ignorance of all sentient beings, drying up the turbid currents of all afflictions, and causing the roots of goodness, merit, and wisdom of all sentient beings to grow and reach maturity.

Although these various manifestations appear simultaneously, they remain eternally serene and unmoving from their original locus; for the Buddha, having already transcended conceptualization and discrimination, naturally manifests these various signs.

“Mañjuśrī! If there were good sons or good daughters who, for as many eons as there are sands in the Ganges, were to offer celestial flavors and exquisite celestial garments to all Buddhas and their assemblies of śrāvakas, as numerous as the atoms within the worlds of the ten directions;”
After that Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, for each and every Buddha, he constructed throughout the ten directions—in every single world—stūpas as numerous as the atoms within the worlds of the ten directions.

These stūpas were all made of Jambūnada gold, interspersed with lightning-flash maṇi jewels; they gathered together various radiant treasures, surrounded by railings, with precious banners erected far and wide, and jeweled bells chiming melodiously. They used sandalwood guarded by serpents as ointment and were covered with nets of sovereign maṇi-kings.

Above these, there were further clouds of celestial jewel canopies, clouds of precious banners and pennants, clouds of exquisite flowers and incense, clouds of *maṇi* kings, and clouds of wish-fulfilling jewels, hovering and dispersing through the sky to fill the trichiliocosm.

If one were to make such offerings three times every day for as many kalpas as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, while simultaneously teaching and transforming countless sentient beings—such offering is not equal to that of a person who, upon hearing this Dharma-door of entering the inconceivable realm of the Tathāgata’s wisdom and virtue, gives rise to faith and understanding; the latter’s merit surpasses the former by immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas.

“Mañjuśrī! If there are bodhisattvas who believe in and understand this Dharma, they will swiftly fulfill immeasurable billions of nayutas of the pāramitās of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva; they will realize and enter immeasurable billions of nayutas of stages; they will turn their backs on and abandon immeasurable billions of nayutas of births and deaths; they will thoroughly know the supernormal powers of immeasurable billions of nayutas of Buddhas; they will shatter immeasurable asaṃkhyeyas of the mountains of self-conceit; they will topple immeasurable asaṃkhyeyas of the banners of stinginess and envy; they will dry up immeasurable asaṃkhyeyas of the rivers of craving; they will cross over immeasurable asaṃkhyeyas of the oceans of birth and death; they will sever immeasurable asaṃkhyeyas of Māra’s nets; and they will eclipse the majestic radiance of all suns, moons, Śakras, Brahmās, and World-Protectors.”
Traveling from one buddha-field to another, they are able to rescue sentient beings suffering in the realms of hell,
hungry ghosts, animals, and King Yama. They constantly draw near to all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, fully accomplishing the Ocean-Seal Samādhi,
the Samādhi of Holding All Dharmas, the Samādhi of Sovereignty over Dharmas, the Samādhi of Adornments of All Marks, and the Jewel-Birth [Samādhi].
The samādhi of equanimity, the samādhi of peace and bliss, the lotus-adornment samādhi, the space-treasury samādhi,
the samādhi of entering according with the world, the samādhi of the exquisite dharma-flower, the samādhi of mastery over the objective realm,
the great valorous stride samādhi, the space-mind samādhi, and the lion’s valorous stride samādhi.
The Sun-Lamp Samādhi, the Immeasurable Revolving Samādhi, the Showering Nectar Samādhi, the Vajra Banner Samādhi,
the Like-Vajra Samādhi, the Vajra-Array Samādhi, the Earth-Support Samādhi, the Sumeru Lamp Samādhi,
the Sumeru Banner Samādhi, the Treasure-Treasury Samādhi, and the Mind-Mastery Samādhi.
The samādhi of [all] samādhis, the samādhi of mastery over the minds of all sentient beings,
the samādhi of increasing all practices, the samādhi of profound and secret skillful means, the samādhi of various eloquences, the samādhi of being invisible to others,
the samādhi of comprehending all dharmas, the samādhi of playful sport, and the samādhi of producing all supernormal powers.
the Samādhi of Subduing Māras, the Samādhi of Manifesting All Physical Forms, the Samādhi of Supreme Excellence in All Physical Forms,
the Samādhi of Contemplating the Body, the Samādhi of Endowing All Practices, the Samādhi of the Lamp of Wisdom, the Samādhi of the Light of Bodhi,
the Samādhi of Eloquence in Joyful Speech, and the Samādhi of Entering All Meritorious Qualities;
He preached the Samādhi of the True Mark of All Dharmas, the Samādhi of Quiescent Supernatural Powers,
the Śūraṅgama Samādhi, and the Ocean Tide Samādhi; furthermore,

he attained the Dharanī of the Physical Marks of Immeasurable Buddhas, the Dharanī of Great Wisdom, the Dharanī of Pure Sound, the Dharanī of the Inexhaustible Casket, the Dharanī of Immeasurable Revolutions, the Dharanī of the Ocean Seal, the Dharanī of Entering Definitive Eloquence, and the Dharanī of the Sustaining Power of All Buddhas.

Furthermore, they attain accordance with all sentient beings, the supreme practice of all dharmas, teacherless wisdom that severs all doubts regarding dharmas, the supernormal powers of a Buddha, and the skillful means of bodhisattva conduct.
“Mañjuśrī! Just as Sumeru, the king of mountains, is lofty, prominent, and beautiful, outshining all other mountains;
so too is it with a bodhisattva who has faith and understanding in this dharma-gate—their merit and purity so outshine the roots of goodness of all sentient beings.”
At that time, Mañjuśrī addressed the Bodhisattva Sarvanivaraṇaviṣkambhin, saying:
"Son of the Buddha!
There is yet another supreme dharma."
"If any bodhisattvas are able to believe and understand this, they will then achieve other superior merits.
Having heard these words, the Bodhisattva Destroyer of All Obscurations addressed Mañjuśrī again, saying:
"If there are bodhisattvas who believe and understand these five dharmas, they will be able to set aside this superior dharma and attain other immeasurable, extraordinary merits."
What are these five?
First, to have faith and understanding that all dharmas are neither arising nor ceasing, ineffable, peerless, and without counterpart;

second, to have faith and understanding that the Tathāgata, through effortless and non-conceptual activity, enters into modes of conduct as numerous as the atoms of Jambudvīpa, constantly arising and never ceasing from moment to moment.

Third, believe that although Śākyamuni Tathāgata taught King Sūtaputra in the past, it was solely for the sake of bringing all sentient beings to maturity; in reality, he attained perfect enlightenment long ago, as many kalpas ago as there are grains of sand in the Ganges.

Fourth, one has faith that from the time Śākyamuni Tathāgata was shown the prediction of enlightenment by Dīpaṃkara Buddha until his attainment of Buddhahood, he practiced the bodhisattva path during that interval; yet in reality, he had already attained equal and perfect enlightenment and dwelt in the realm of the Buddhas for immeasurable kalpas.

Fifth, one has faith that although the Tathāgata Śākyamuni currently relies upon a royal palace and the Śākya clan is being harmed, this is solely for the purpose of bringing all sentient beings to maturity; in reality, he has already attained equal and perfect enlightenment since immeasurable kalpas past.
“Mañjuśrī! If a bodhisattva can develop faith and understanding in these five kinds [of teachings], they will be able to set aside this supreme dharma and further achieve other supreme merits.”

“Mañjuśrī! If a son of good family or a daughter of good family were, for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, to daily offer celestial food of a hundred flavors and celestial exquisite garments to as many Arhats throughout the worlds of the ten directions as there are motes of dust—Arhats who possess the six supernormal powers and the eight liberations—the merit they would obtain would not equal that of someone who, in a single day, offers food and drink to a single Pratyekabuddha; the latter’s merit would surpass the former by incalculable times.”
"Furthermore, Mañjuśrī!

If a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to construct throughout the worlds of the ten directions as many monasteries as there are motes of dust in those worlds for incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) *pratyekabuddhas* and others—each monastery made entirely of Jāmbūnada gold, with pillars of *maṇi* gems, and stairways, railings, pavilions, doors, and windows all adorned with various kinds of jewels; provided with great jeweled canopies and smeared with exquisite sandalwood;

and if they were to reverently make offerings of celestial food of a hundred flavors and celestial fine garments every day for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges—this would not equal the merit obtained by someone who hears the name of a Buddha, or the name of a World-Honored One (*bhagavat*), or the name of a Tathāgata, or the name of the All-Knowing One (*sarvajña*, *sarvajñatā*), which exceeds that [previous merit] by incalculable times."
How much more so for those who create images of the Tathāgata through painting or molding with clay; those who behold them gain merit many times greater than that, beyond measure (asaṃkhyeya).
How much more so for those who offer various kinds of worship with lamps, incense, flowers, music, and the like; their merit is again many times greater than that, beyond measure.

How much more so for one who, within the Buddha-dharma, is able to protect and uphold even a single precept for as little as one day; their merit would exceed that by incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) times. "Mañjuśrī!..."

If there were good sons or good daughters who, for as many eons as there are sands in the Ganges River, daily provided celestial food of a hundred flavors and celestial exquisite garments to Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and the assembly of Śrāvakas, as numerous as the atoms within the worlds of the ten directions;

After the parinirvāṇa of each of the Buddhas, one might build for each of them stupas as numerous as the atoms in the worlds of the ten directions, with each stupa being as large as the four continents, of exquisite design and adorned with myriad jewels, featuring banners, canopies, music, and all manner of superior offerings—yet if one has not yet attained faith and understanding in this Dharma-gate, even though they possess all such merits, they are not equal to someone who can believe and understand this Dharma-gate of entering the inconceivable realm of the Tathāgata’s wisdom and virtue; even if that person merely gives a single morsel of food to an animal, their merit exceeds the former by incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) times.

“Mañjuśrī! If there is a bodhisattva who believes and understands this sūtra and makes offerings to the Buddhas as described therein, and another bodhisattva, having heard it, rejoices and gives rise to pure faith, rising from their seat with palms joined in salutation and practicing offerings according to their capacity, the merit of the latter exceeds that of the former by incalculable times, because such a person will before long attain the wisdom of a Buddha.”

When this sutra was being spoken, those bhikṣus and the assembly of bodhisattvas, as well as all the world’s devas, humans, asuras, and others, rejoiced, accepted it with faith, prostrated, and practiced accordingly.
The Vaipulya Scripture on Entering the Inconceivable Wisdom and Virtue of the Tathāgata.
